questions.q: A 35-year-old male presents with a painless, indurated ulcer on the glans penis for 2 weeks. Inguinal lymph nodes are firm, non-tender, and rubbery. VDRL is reactive at 1:32. Which statement about treatment is MOST accurate?
opts: Benzathine penicillin 2.4 million units IM single dose is curative for primary syphilis
Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days is first-line therapy
Azithromycin 2g single dose is equivalent to penicillin for all stages
Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM single dose is the WHO-recommended first-line treatment
questions.exp: Primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis (<1 year) are treated with benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM as a single dose. Doxycycline is an alternative in penicillin-allergic patients. Azithromycin resistance is now widespread and it is NOT recommended as equivalent to penicillin.

questions.q: A 28-year-old immunocompetent patient presents with multiple grouped vesicles on an erythematous base along the right T5 dermatome. Three days later, new lesions continue to appear. The MOST appropriate antiviral regimen is:
opts: Acyclovir 200 mg five times daily for 5 days
Valacyclovir 1g three times daily for 7 days
Famciclovir 250 mg three times daily for 5 days
Acyclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7 days
questions.exp: Herpes zoster in an immunocompetent host is treated with acyclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7 days OR valacyclovir 1g TID for 7 days OR famciclovir 500 mg TID for 7 days. Acyclovir 200 mg five times daily is the dose for herpes simplex, not zoster. Option D is the standard oral acyclovir dose for zoster.

questions.q: A 40-year-old farmer from Gujarat presents with a chronic, progressive, swollen right foot with multiple sinuses discharging black granules. The MOST likely causative organism is:
questions.exp: Madura foot (mycetoma) in India is most commonly caused by Madurella mycetomatis, which produces black granules. Nocardia and Actinomadura produce white-yellow granules. The black granule is the key distinguishing feature pointing to Madurella mycetomatis (eumycetoma).

questions.q: A 6-year-old child presents with a well-demarcated hypopigmented patch on the cheek with fine scales. Woods lamp examination shows no enhancement. The MOST likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Pityriasis alba presents as ill-defined to well-demarcated hypopigmented patches with fine scales, typically on the face of children. It does NOT fluoresce on Wood's lamp. Vitiligo shows bright white fluorescence. Pityriasis versicolor shows golden-yellow fluorescence. Tinea faciei usually shows erythema and scaling in a different pattern.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman on long-term hydroxychloroquine for lupus presents with decreased visual acuity. Fundoscopy reveals bull's eye maculopathy. The pathological basis of this toxicity is:
opts: Blockade of VEGF leading to retinal ischemia
Accumulation of drug in melanin-containing cells of the retinal pigment epithelium
Immune complex deposition in retinal vasculature
questions.exp: Hydroxychloroquine binds to melanin in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and accumulates over time, causing progressive toxicity manifesting as bull's eye maculopathy. This is why patients require annual ophthalmology screening after 5 years of use. The dose should be <5 mg/kg/day to minimize risk.

questions.q: A 32-year-old male leprosy patient on multidrug therapy (MDT) develops sudden fever, erythema nodosum-like tender red nodules over the extremities, uveitis, and testicular swelling. The correct immediate management is:
opts: Stop all MDT and start systemic steroids
Continue MDT and add thalidomide 100-300 mg daily
Continue MDT and add prednisolone with supportive care
questions.exp: This describes Type 2 lepra reaction (Erythema Nodosum Leprosum - ENL). Thalidomide is the drug of choice for severe ENL. MDT must NEVER be stopped during lepra reactions. Thalidomide 100-300 mg/day is highly effective for ENL. Prednisolone is used when thalidomide is contraindicated (females of childbearing age). Clofazimine at higher doses also has anti-ENL activity.

questions.q: A skin biopsy from a patient with chronic stable plaque psoriasis shows elongated rete ridges, thinning of suprapapillary plates, dilated tortuous capillaries in dermal papillae, and collections of neutrophils in the stratum corneum. These neutrophil collections are called:
questions.exp: Collections of neutrophils in the stratum corneum of psoriatic skin are called Munro microabscesses. Kogoj spongiform pustules are collections of neutrophils in the stratum spinosum/malpighii layer. Pautrier microabscesses (collections of atypical lymphocytes) are seen in mycosis fungoides. These are distinct histopathological findings.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with recurrent oral ulcers, genital ulcers, and anterior uveitis for 2 years. She also has a positive pathergy test. The underlying immunological mechanism is:
opts: Type I hypersensitivity with IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation
Type II hypersensitivity with antibody-mediated cytotoxicity
Neutrophil hyperactivation with dysregulation of innate and adaptive immunity
Type IV hypersensitivity with CD8+ T cell-mediated cytotoxicity
questions.exp: Behcet's disease is characterized by neutrophil hyperactivation and dysregulation of both innate and adaptive immunity. The pathergy test (hyperreactivity to minor trauma) reflects neutrophil hyperfunction. There is increased neutrophil chemotaxis and oxidative burst, elevated TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, and IL-6. HLA-B51 is strongly associated.

questions.q: A 60-year-old woman presents with tense bullae on normal skin and mildly inflamed skin. Nikolsky sign is negative. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 deposition at the dermoepidermal junction. Indirect immunofluorescence on salt-split skin shows deposits on the roof (epidermal side). The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) shows linear IgG and C3 at BMZ on DIF. On salt-split skin, BP antibodies bind to the roof (epidermal side) because the target antigens BPAG1 (BP230) and BPAG2 (BP180/collagen XVII) are in the hemidesmosome on the epidermal side of the split. EBA and anti-p200 pemphigoid bind to the floor (dermal side).

questions.q: A 25-year-old male presents with a rapidly growing nodule on the dorsum of the hand for 6 weeks. It is 1.5 cm, dome-shaped, with a central keratin-filled crater. Biopsy shows a well-differentiated squamous proliferation with a central keratinous plug, glassy eosinophilic cytoplasm, and an inverted flask-shaped architecture. The BEST management is:
opts: Observation as most keratoacanthomas spontaneously regress
Complete surgical excision to obtain histological margins and exclude SCC
questions.exp: While keratoacanthoma (KA) may spontaneously regress, the standard of care is complete surgical excision. This is because KA cannot be reliably distinguished from well-differentiated SCC clinically or histologically, and some pathologists consider KA a variant of SCC. Excision provides a definitive diagnosis and clear margins. Observation carries the risk of missing an invasive SCC.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman on methotrexate for psoriasis develops macrocytic anaemia, oral ulcers, and elevated liver enzymes. Which folic acid supplementation schedule is MOST appropriate to prevent methotrexate toxicity while maintaining efficacy?
opts: Folinic acid 5 mg on the same day as methotrexate
Folic acid 1 mg daily every day of the week
Folic acid 5 mg once weekly on a day different from methotrexate
Folic acid 5 mg daily on all days except the day of methotrexate
questions.exp: Folic acid 5 mg once weekly, taken on a day other than the methotrexate dose day, reduces methotrexate toxicity (GI, hepatic, haematological) without significantly reducing its anti-psoriatic efficacy. Folic acid on the same day as methotrexate may reduce efficacy. Folinic acid (leucovorin) is used for methotrexate rescue in toxicity, not routine supplementation.

questions.q: A 30-year-old HIV-positive patient (CD4 count 80 cells/microL) presents with warty cauliflower-like perianal lesions that are rapidly growing. Biopsy shows koilocytes, parakeratosis, and high-grade dysplasia with full-thickness atypia. The HPV type MOST likely responsible is:
questions.exp: HPV 16 (and HPV 18) are high-risk oncogenic types responsible for anogenital squamous cell carcinoma and its precursor lesions (high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions - HSIL). HPV 6 and 11 are low-risk types causing condyloma acuminata (genital warts). In immunosuppressed patients, high-risk HPV types cause aggressive disease with malignant transformation.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with bilateral symmetrical butterfly-shaped erythema over the malar area, photosensitivity, and joint pain. ANA is positive at 1:640, anti-dsDNA is positive, and complement levels (C3, C4) are low. The most specific antibody for this condition is:
questions.exp: Anti-Smith (anti-Sm) antibodies are the MOST specific antibody for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), present in ~25-30% of cases. Anti-dsDNA is sensitive and specific and correlates with disease activity. Anti-Ro/SS-A is associated with SLE, Sjogren's, neonatal lupus, and subacute cutaneous lupus. Anti-histone antibodies are characteristic of drug-induced lupus.

questions.q: A 40-year-old farmer presents with recurrent boils and furunculosis. Culture grows Staphylococcus aureus that tests positive for Panton-Valentine Leukocidin (PVL) gene. This toxin primarily targets:
opts: Neutrophils and macrophages causing leukocyte lysis
questions.exp: Panton-Valentine Leukocidin (PVL) is a two-component toxin produced by community-associated MRSA (CA-MRSA) that targets and lyses neutrophils and macrophages, enabling the bacteria to evade innate immune defenses. This explains the severe, recurrent skin and soft tissue infections (furunculosis, carbuncles, necrotizing pneumonia) associated with PVL-positive strains.

questions.q: A 22-year-old patient presents with multiple annular, scaly plaques on the trunk with central clearing. KOH mount shows branching septate hyphae. Cultures grow a colony that is initially white and becomes tan/buff-colored with a powdery texture. The causative organism is:
questions.exp: Trichophyton rubrum is the most common cause of tinea corporis worldwide. Its colonies are white initially, becoming tan-buff with a powdery or granular texture, and red/wine-red on the reverse side. Microsporum canis produces club-shaped macroconidia with thick walls. T. violaceum has deep violet/purple pigmentation. Epidermophyton floccosum lacks microconidia and produces smooth-walled macroconidia.

questions.q: A 65-year-old male smoker presents with a chronic non-healing ulcer on the lower lip. Biopsy shows invasive nests of squamous cells with keratin pearls extending into the dermis. Sentinel lymph node biopsy is positive. The T stage based on tumor size of 2.5 cm is:
questions.exp: Per AJCC 8th edition staging for lip and oral cavity SCC: T1 = <=2 cm, T2 = >2 cm but <=4 cm, T3 = >4 cm, T4a = moderately advanced local disease. A tumor of 2.5 cm falls in the T2 category. The positive sentinel node makes this at least N1. Lip SCC has a higher risk of nodal metastasis than non-lip cutaneous SCC.

questions.q: An 18-year-old presents with clustered papulovesicles on the elbows and buttocks with intense pruritus. Skin biopsy shows neutrophilic microabscesses at dermal papillae tips. Direct immunofluorescence shows granular IgA deposits at the DEJ. The MOST appropriate investigation to confirm underlying disease is:
opts: Anti-endomysial IgA antibodies with small bowel biopsy
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is the cutaneous manifestation of celiac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy). Granular IgA at DEJ on DIF is pathognomonic. Anti-endomysial antibodies and anti-tTG IgA are highly sensitive/specific; however, the gold standard for confirming underlying celiac disease is small bowel biopsy showing villous atrophy. Both anti-endomysial and small bowel biopsy together give definitive confirmation.

questions.q: A 70-year-old woman on captopril for hypertension for 3 months presents with sudden onset massive edematous swelling of lips and tongue, causing airway compromise. There is no urticaria. C1-inhibitor levels and complement C4 are both low. The mechanism of this reaction is:
opts: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation releasing histamine
Inhibition of ACE leading to bradykinin accumulation
Direct mast cell activation by ACE inhibitor
Complement activation through the lectin pathway
questions.exp: ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema is bradykinin-mediated, NOT histamine-mediated. ACE (kininase II) normally degrades bradykinin. When ACE is inhibited, bradykinin accumulates, causing increased vascular permeability and angioedema. It does NOT respond to antihistamines or adrenaline. Treatment is with icatibant (bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist), C1-esterase inhibitor concentrate, or fresh frozen plasma.

questions.q: A 28-year-old male presents with a 3 cm violaceous, firm papule on the upper arm. Dermoscopy shows a central white scar-like area with peripheral brown globules in a starburst pattern. The MOST likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Spitz naevus shows the starburst pattern on dermoscopy - a central white-to-pink area with symmetric, regular streaks/globules radiating at the periphery like a starburst. This pattern is distinct from the typical ring pattern of dermatofibroma (central white scar + peripheral pigment network) and blue naevus (homogeneous blue-white veil). In adults, Spitz naevus requires complete excision due to difficulty distinguishing from spitzoid melanoma.

questions.q: A leprosy patient on clofazimine for 18 months develops ichthyosis-like skin changes, discoloration of the skin (reddish-brown), and similar discoloration of urine. The underlying mechanism of clofazimine's anti-bacterial activity is:
opts: Binding to mycobacterial DNA and inhibiting RNA transcription
Inhibition of cell wall mycolic acid synthesis
Inhibition of 30S ribosomal subunit protein synthesis
questions.exp: Clofazimine is a riminophenazine dye that binds to mycobacterial DNA and inhibits template function for RNA polymerase (inhibits RNA transcription). It also has anti-inflammatory properties through inhibition of neutrophil function (useful in ENL). Side effects include reddish-brown skin discoloration (due to drug deposition in macrophages), ichthyosis, conjunctival pigmentation, and GI upset.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with progressive dysphagia, tightening of skin over the face and hands for 3 years. Skin biopsy shows dense collagen deposition in the reticular dermis with loss of adnexal structures. The antibody associated with the WORST prognosis (pulmonary hypertension and scleroderma renal crisis) is:
questions.exp: Anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies are associated with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (dcSSc) and carry the highest risk of scleroderma renal crisis (SRC). They are also associated with rapid skin progression. Anti-Scl-70 is associated with ILD (interstitial lung disease). ACA (anti-centromere) is associated with limited cutaneous SSc (CREST syndrome) and pulmonary arterial hypertension. Anti-U1-RNP is associated with Mixed Connective Tissue Disease.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male presents with a well-defined pearly, translucent nodule with telangiectasias on the nasolabial fold. It has been slowly growing for 2 years. He is a farmer with significant sun exposure. The gold standard treatment with the lowest recurrence rate is:
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) of the face, especially in high-risk locations (nasolabial fold, periorbital, periauricular areas - the 'H-zone'), is best treated with Mohs micrographic surgery (MMS). MMS provides real-time margin control with tissue conservation, achieving the lowest recurrence rate (~1% for primary BCC). Standard excision with 4 mm margins is appropriate for low-risk truncal BCCs.

questions.q: A 30-year-old male presents with diffuse hair loss. Pull test is positive (>6 hairs per pull). Trichoscopy reveals yellow dots, empty follicular units, and short vellus hairs. This pattern is consistent with:
questions.exp: Trichoscopy of alopecia areata classically shows yellow dots (dilated follicular infundibula filled with sebum/keratinous material), black dots (cadaverized hairs), broken hairs, exclamation mark hairs, and short vellus hairs. Telogen effluvium shows increased telogen hairs (white dots at follicular ostia) without yellow dots. Androgenetic alopecia shows follicular miniaturization (variability in hair shaft diameter) with peripilar sign.

questions.q: A 14-year-old girl presents with nail pitting, onycholysis, and oil spots (salmon patches) in the nails. She has no skin lesions. The probability of psoriatic arthritis in a patient with isolated nail psoriasis compared to one with skin psoriasis is:
opts: The same as skin psoriasis patients
Nail involvement is not associated with psoriatic arthritis
questions.exp: Nail psoriasis is an independent predictor of psoriatic arthritis (PsA). Patients with nail psoriasis have a significantly higher risk of developing PsA compared to those with skin-only psoriasis. The NAPSI (Nail Psoriasis Severity Index) score correlates with PsA risk. Nail matrix disease (pitting, leukonychia) and nail bed disease (onycholysis, oil spots, subungual hyperkeratosis) both increase PsA risk.

questions.q: A 20-year-old pregnant woman (16 weeks) presents with a mildly pruritic annular erythematous plaque with peripheral scaling. The MOST important consideration in management is:
opts: Avoiding systemic antifungals as they are teratogenic
Topical clotrimazole is safe and effective
Oral griseofulvin can be used after first trimester
Systemic terbinafine is the drug of choice in pregnancy
questions.exp: Tinea corporis in pregnancy is managed with topical antifungals. Clotrimazole (and other topical azoles) and topical terbinafine are safe for use in pregnancy. Systemic antifungals should be avoided: griseofulvin is contraindicated (teratogenic - Category X), oral azoles (fluconazole at high doses associated with birth defects), and terbinafine has limited safety data. Topical treatment is the first-line approach.

questions.q: During a Tzanck smear from the floor of a fresh blister in pemphigus vulgaris, the characteristic finding is:
questions.exp: Tzanck smear from pemphigus vulgaris shows acantholytic cells (Tzanck cells) - rounded cells with large hyperchromatic nuclei and scant cytoplasm that have lost their intercellular attachments due to anti-desmoglein antibodies causing acantholysis. Multinucleated giant cells are seen in herpes virus infections. Clue cells are seen in bacterial vaginosis. Eosinophils predominate in bullous pemphigoid.

questions.q: A 35-year-old male presents with yellowish-brown scaly plaques in the axilla, groin, and inframammary folds. Wood's lamp examination shows coral-red fluorescence. The organism responsible produces which enzyme that gives the fluorescence?
opts: Coproporphyrin III produced during bacterial metabolism under Wood's lamp
Corynebacterium minutissimum produces water-soluble porphyrins (coproporphyrin III)
questions.exp: Erythrasma is caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum. The coral-red fluorescence under Wood's lamp (365 nm) is due to water-soluble porphyrins (specifically coproporphyrin III) produced by the bacteria. The fluorescence is present only in fresh lesions; washing removes the water-soluble porphyrins. Treatment is topical erythromycin or fusidic acid, or oral erythromycin for extensive cases.

questions.q: A 48-year-old male presents with recurrent non-scarring alopecia patches, exclamation mark hairs, and spontaneous regrowth. He also has features suggesting Down syndrome. The association between alopecia areata and Down syndrome is explained by:
opts: Trisomy 21 causing increased androgen sensitivity in hair follicles
Increased expression of autoimmune susceptibility genes on chromosome 21
Down syndrome-related thyroid dysfunction causing hair loss
Seborrheic dermatitis-related follicular damage common in Down syndrome
questions.exp: Alopecia areata (AA) is an autoimmune T-cell mediated condition. Its association with Down syndrome is due to increased expression of genes encoding immune regulatory molecules on chromosome 21, particularly DYRK1A and HMGN1, contributing to immune dysregulation. The incidence of AA in Down syndrome is 60-fold higher than the general population. AA is associated with multiple autoimmune conditions.

questions.q: A 30-year-old male with type 2 leprosy reaction (ENL) is being treated with thalidomide. The MOST serious teratogenic effect of thalidomide affecting the fetus if taken during weeks 4-8 of gestation is:
questions.exp: Thalidomide's most infamous teratogenic effect is phocomelia - severe limb reduction defects (flipper-like or absent limbs) when taken during weeks 4-8 of pregnancy, the critical period for limb bud development. This was responsible for the thalidomide tragedy of the 1950s-60s. Thalidomide is absolutely contraindicated in women of childbearing potential without strict contraception (STEPS program in USA).

questions.q: A 25-year-old male presents with grouped vesicles on the shaft of the penis with burning pain. He reports a similar episode 6 months ago. Which protein allows herpes simplex virus to establish latency in sensory ganglia?
questions.exp: HSV establishes lifelong latency in sensory dorsal root ganglia. The Latency-Associated Transcripts (LATs) are the only viral genes abundantly expressed during latency. LATs block apoptosis of infected neurons, suppress lytic cycle gene expression, and maintain latency. Reactivation is triggered by stimuli such as UV light, fever, stress, and immunosuppression, causing recurrent mucocutaneous disease.

questions.q: A 50-year-old female presents with anti-MDA5 antibody-positive dermatomyositis. This antibody is particularly associated with:
opts: Rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease with poor prognosis
questions.exp: Anti-MDA5 (melanoma differentiation-associated gene 5, also called anti-CADM-140) antibodies in dermatomyositis are strongly associated with rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease (RP-ILD), which carries a very poor prognosis with high mortality. These patients often have clinically amyopathic dermatomyositis (CADM) with skin features but minimal muscle weakness. Aggressive immunosuppression is required.
